title: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn

Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn
This survey traces the extraordinary figure of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the sixth Rebbe of Chabad Hasidism, who led his people in one of the most turbulent periods of the twentieth century. The text sketches the leader's dramatic passage between worlds, from running an underground Torah network in the face of the cruel persecutions of the Soviet regime to rebuilding the world of Judaism on American soil under the revolutionary call that "America is no different." Across the chapters a rare combination is revealed of firm religious conservatism and sophisticated use of modern tools to spread the message of Hasidism, with emphasis on the value of self-sacrifice as a central axis of his personality. The source seeks to present not only the biography of the Rayatz but also his rich Torah and literary teaching, which turned Hasidism from a local Eastern European movement into a living global spiritual force.
Strength and Fortitude: The Life, Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn
Preface: Leadership in the Shadow of the Crises of the Twentieth Century
The figure of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the sixth Rebbe in the Chabad-Lubavitch dynasty (known as the Rayatz), constitutes a historical and spiritual crossroads without equal in the history of Israel in the modern era. The period of his leadership, which extended over the years 5680–5711 (1920–1950), coincided with the most dramatic upheavals that befell the Jewish people: from the destruction of the spiritual centers of Eastern Europe under the Soviet and Nazi boot to the beginning of the building of the world of Torah in the United States and in the Land of Israel.[1, 2, 3] The Rayatz was not merely the heir of a glorious dynasty; he was the architect of a global system of reconstruction, a leader who succeeded in preserving the ember of Judaism under impossible underground conditions in the Soviet Union, and at the same time in replanting it in the modern and secular soil of the Western world.[4, 5, 6]
An in-depth analysis of his work reveals a rare combination of uncompromising religious conservatism and a phenomenological understanding of modern tools. Whereas many religious leaders tended to shut themselves off in the face of modernity, the Rayatz harnessed the most modern tools of his time – the press, printing technology and methods of organizational management – in order to spread the message of Hasidism to the masses.[3, 7, 8] His Torah teaching, which combines deep theoretical discourses, stirring talks of moral instruction and historiographical memoirs, created a bridge between the "old world" and the new Jewish reality, while setting the concept of "mesirut nefesh" (self-sacrifice) not merely as an abstract religious value but as a political and social way of life.[9, 10, 11]
Chapter 1: The Formative Years and the Leadership of the Tomchei Temimim Yeshiva
Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak was born on 12 Tammuz 5640 (1880) in the town of Lubavitch, the only son of the fifth Rebbe, Rabbi Shalom Dovber (the Rashab), and Sterna Sarah.[1, 12] From his childhood he was trained for the role of leadership; at the age of only 12 he experienced his first arrest after defending a Jewish merchant from the heavy hand of a Russian policeman – an event that marked his readiness to stand up to the authorities for the sake of another.[3] At the age of 15 he was appointed his father's personal secretary, a position that exposed him to the corridors of the Tsarist government and to the public struggles of Russian Jewry.[2, 9, 13]
The most significant turning point in shaping his administrative and educational character came in the year 5657 (1897), the year of his marriage to Nechama Dina Schneersohn.[9, 12] During the days of the "Sheva Berakhot" (the seven days of wedding celebration), his father announced the founding of the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva and appointed his son as its acting director.[7, 14, 15] This yeshiva was a pedagogical revolution; it required the students (who were called "Temimim") to combine theoretical study of the Talmud ("nigleh," the revealed) with systematic study of the teaching of Hasidism ("nistar," the hidden), with emphasis on the spiritual work of refining the character traits and on lengthy prayer.[3, 7, 14]
Under his leadership Tomchei Temimim became a worldwide network, but beyond dry administration the Rayatz created a model of "soldiers of the House of David" – young people personally committed to preserving Judaism at any price.[3, 7] His experience in running institutions under the watchful eye of the Tsarist secret police (which arrested him four times between 1902 and 1911 because of his public activity) was in effect the practical apprenticeship for the great and bitter struggle against the Communist regime.[2, 13, 15]
Chapter 2: The Underground Campaign in the Soviet Union (1920–1927)
With the passing of his father on 2 Nisan 5680 (1920), the Rayatz took upon himself the yoke of leadership at the most difficult hour of Russian Jewry.[9, 12] The Bolshevik Revolution created a reality in which religion was declared the "opium of the masses," and the "Yevsektsiya" (the Jewish section of the Communist Party) acted cruelly to destroy every sign of Jewish life.[2, 4, 5] Whereas many public leaders chose to leave Russia, the Rayatz declared that "the Schneersohns do not flee" and conducted a world-embracing underground war.[4, 6]
The Rayatz set up a system of "a state within a state" that operated in complete secrecy. This network included hundreds of "chadarim" (Talmud Torah schools) in cellars, wandering yeshivot, mikvaot built at night and ritual slaughterers who worked in secret.[2, 4, 6, 16] He did not only instruct others to sacrifice themselves, but stood at the front; in 1924, at the height of the persecutions in Moscow, he made a covenant with a group of young men in which they promised to fight for the preservation of Judaism to the last drop of their blood.[6] This activity of his extended from the urban centers of Leningrad and Rostov to distant regions such as Bukhara, Georgia and Dagestan.[2, 6, 13]
The link between his underground leadership and his Torah teaching found expression in the concept of "bittul" (self-nullification). According to the Rayatz, Jewish survival under a totalitarian regime cannot be based on tactical compromises, but on a deep inner recognition that the divine law stands above every decree of flesh and blood.[4, 9] He instructed his Hasidim to ignore fear; when he was asked by a Tsarist officer what he would do if he were imprisoned, he answered dismissively that the body is indeed subject to the government, but the soul is free forever.[6] This approach created a generation of Hasidim who were ready to be sent to Siberia or to stand before a firing squad as long as they did not close the local "cheder".[5, 6, 16]
Chapter 3: Shpalerka and Kostroma – The Imprisonment That Became a Festival
The direct confrontation with the Soviet government reached its peak on 15 Sivan 5687 (1927). Following informing by the Yevsektsiya, the Rayatz was arrested in his home in Leningrad and taken to the notorious "Shpalerka" prison.[2, 9, 17] He was accused of counter-revolutionary activity, and at a certain stage was sentenced to death without trial.[2, 4, 9] Even inside the cell the Rayatz continued to display firm resolve; he refused to answer his interrogators' questions until he was allowed to put on tefillin and pray, and in the end he prevailed – the tefillin were brought to him in his cell.[7, 17]
The imprisonment aroused an international storm. The heavy pressure exerted by the governments of Latvia and Germany, together with the intervention of the International Red Cross, forced the Soviets to commute his sentence.[2, 4, 9] The sentence was changed to exile in the city of Kostroma, and in the end, on 12–13 Tammuz 5687, the Rayatz was released completely.[9, 11, 16] These days were established in Chabad Hasidism as the "Festival of Redemption" (Chag HaGeulah), marking the victory of the spirit over the physical might of the Soviet power.[7, 11, 18]
The consequences of the imprisonment went beyond the physical release. The Rayatz saw these days as a preparation for the future redemption, and determined that this redemption belongs to every Jew wherever he may be, even to one who is only "called by the name of Israel".[11] This event fixed in Hasidic consciousness the idea that even in the face of utter darkness, a single Jew can light a light that will illuminate the whole world.[18]
Chapter 4: Journeys and Revelations – From the Land of Israel to America (1928–1940)
After his expulsion from the Soviet Union, the Rayatz moved to Riga in Latvia, where he founded a yeshiva and continued to direct the Russian underground from afar.[2, 4, 8] In the year 5689 (1929) he made a historic fifteen-day journey in the Land of Israel.[2, 14] His visit had deep spiritual and political significance; he visited the communities of Hebron, Jerusalem, Safed and Tiberias, and even succeeded in entering the Cave of the Patriarchs – a visit that was almost impossible for Jews at that time.[2, 14, 19] The journey ended a few days before the Hebron massacre, an event in which several of his disciples and close friends were murdered.[2, 19]
From there the Rayatz went on to a long journey in the United States (1929–1930). The aim of the journey was twofold: raising funds for the reconstruction of the Jewry of Europe and Russia, and examining the potential for moving the center of Hasidism to America.[2, 20, 21] He was received with royal honors, hosted mayors and politicians, and even met with President Herbert Hoover at the White House.[20, 21] Despite the sympathy, he was shocked by the low spiritual state he found there; the notion of the "melting pot" threatened to swallow up the remnants of the tradition of the Jewish immigrants.[20, 22]
In 1934 the Rayatz settled in Poland, first in Warsaw and later in Otwock.[8, 15] There he set up an extensive network of yeshivot and founded the journal "HaTamim," which served as a central platform for Torah scholarship.[8, 10, 15] With the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939, the Rayatz refused to abandon his Hasidim in bombed Warsaw, and remained in the city during the siege and the surrender to the Nazis.[15, 23] Only after enormous diplomatic efforts, which involved the American State Department and German intelligence officers who acted under pressure, was the Rayatz rescued from the inferno, and he arrived in New York on 9 Adar II 5700 (1940).[3, 4, 8, 15]
Chapter 5: The American Revolution – "America Is No Different"
The arrival of the Rayatz in America marked the beginning of a new era in world Jewry. He arrived as a refugee, broken in body and confined to a wheelchair, but in spirit he was more determined than ever.[7, 15, 16] When voices were heard claiming that he should content himself with running a small, closed community because "America is different," he made his immortal declaration: "America is no different!" (Amerika iz nisht andersh!).[3, 16, 24] This call was not merely a theological declaration but a radical program of work for changing the face of American Judaism.[3]
He immediately established the world Chabad headquarters in the building at 770 Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn and founded an unprecedented organizational apparatus [3, 8, 14]:
Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch (Center for Educational Affairs): a body responsible for establishing schools and yeshivot for children and youth.[3, 8]
Machne Israel: an arm for strengthening the observance of the commandments among the general public and for spiritual awakening.[3, 8]
Kehot (Karnei Hod Torah): a publishing house that became one of the largest in the Jewish world, with the aim of spreading Hasidism in every language.[3, 8]
The Rayatz recognized that in America the key was the young generation and women. He set up the "Beit Rivkah" and "Beit Sarah" networks of schools for girls, and founded "Achei Temimim" for children.[3, 8] He encouraged women to take an active part in religious life and in the education of the Jewish home, understanding that they are the pillar of the survival of the tradition.[22] At the same time he initiated social and spiritual activity among Jewish soldiers in the United States Army during the war, and sent the first "shluchim" (emissaries) to remote towns to build mikvaot and to strengthen Sabbath observance.[8, 21, 22]
Chapter 6: His Torah Teaching – Depth and Accessibility
The teaching of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak is a rich mosaic that combines the classic Hasidic discourses with an innovative literary style of story and memoir.[10, 25] Unlike his predecessors, who wrote mainly in the Holy Tongue and in an intricate theoretical style, the Rayatz made extensive use of spoken Yiddish and of vivid descriptions in order to bring the ideas of Hasidism close to the hearts of his listeners.[10, 11]
Sefer HaMaamarim and the Explanations of Hasidism
The core of his work is "Sefer HaMaamarim" (The Book of Discourses), which extends over some 25 volumes.[10, 25] These discourses were delivered on Sabbaths and festivals throughout the thirty years of his leadership. The Rayatz focused on explaining concepts such as "the service of prayer," "the refinement of the body" and "attachment to the tzaddik".[10] He developed a methodology of making the abstract concepts of "Kabbalah" accessible as tools of practical psychology – how a person can change his nature and become a vessel for divine inspiration even within the material world.[11, 22]
Likkutei Dibburim and Sefer HaSichot
The series "Likkutei Dibburim" (5 volumes) is considered the foundational book of "Hasidic guidance" in our generation.[10, 25] In these talks, delivered at farbrengens (Hasidic gatherings), the Rayatz combines stories of tzaddikim, Chabad history and deep spiritual guidance.[10, 25] He believed that the Hasidic story is not merely a tale but a spiritual "surgical instrument" that enables the listener to identify with exemplary figures and to draw from them strength to withstand the trials of the time.[10, 23]
The Long Letter and "Kuntres Divrei Yemei HaChozrim"
The Rayatz was a tireless chronicler. In writings such as "the Long Letter" to his daughter Chaya Mushka or "Kuntres Divrei Yemei HaChozrim" (A Pamphlet of the Chronicles of the Chozrim), he unfolded the unwritten history of Chabad Hasidism, revealing details about the "chozrim" (those who memorized and repeated the words of the Rebbes) and about traditions that passed orally from generation to generation.[10] This activity created a "bridge of memory" that enabled the Hasidim in America to feel part of the chain of generations that had been severed in Europe.[23, 24]
Chapter 7: The Holocaust and the Theology of Redemption
During the years of the war and the Holocaust, from his wheelchair in New York, the Rayatz conducted a spiritual and organizational campaign to rescue European Jewry.[8, 15] He was among the few leaders who cried out even before the outbreak of the war about the terrible danger hovering over Polish Jewry.[3] Under his leadership the Chabad headquarters became a center for gathering information and aiding refugees, in cooperation with bodies such as "Agudat Israel" and the "Red Cross".[2, 8]
His theology in this period focused on the call: "Immediately to repentance – immediately to redemption" (Le-altar li-teshuvah – le-altar li-geulah).[26, 27] The Rayatz saw in the war and the destruction the "birth pangs of the Messiah" and argued that the Jewish people must awaken to repentance in order to hasten the End.[26] He did not content himself with an ideological call but initiated the writing of "the Torah Scroll of the Messiah" – a Torah scroll intended to welcome the Messiah, as a symbolic and practical act expressing complete confidence in the imminent redemption.[11, 26]
Later academic analysis points out that the Rayatz adopted a traditional position of "tziduk ha-din" (the justification of divine judgment), according to which "sin is the cause of all suffering," a call intended to move the masses of Jews in America to change their way of life.[27] Nevertheless, his successor, the Lubavitcher Rebbe, later developed a more complex approach that saw the Holocaust as an event going beyond the bounds of reward and punishment, but the foundations of the active redemptive conception were all laid by the Rayatz.[27]
Chapter 8: His Attitude to the Land of Israel and to Zionism
The Rayatz's attitude to Zionism was a direct continuation of the line taken by his father, the Rashab – ideological opposition to Zionism as a secular political movement that regards itself as the solution to the Jewish problem without connection to Torah and the commandments.[19, 28] He rejected the conception that the establishment of the state is "Atchalta de-Geulah" (the beginning of the redemption) in the religious sense of the term.[28]
Nevertheless, unlike other anti-Zionist streams, the Rayatz showed immense love for the Land of Israel and worked tirelessly for its settlement by observant Jews.[7, 8, 14] He saw to the strengthening of the old communities in Hebron and Jerusalem, established educational institutions in the Land, and after the establishment of the state, in the year 5709 (1949), he founded the village of "Kfar Chabad" near Tel Aviv for refugees from Russia.[8, 12, 14] His vision was to establish in the Land of Israel centers of "Torah and work" that would serve as a spiritual lighthouse for the whole world.[3, 8]
His relations with the leaders of the Yishuv were complex; he maintained a deep friendship with figures such as Zalman Shazar (later President of the State), but never gave up his principled positions on matters of religion and state.[28] He saw in the new state an enormous potential for a mass return to Judaism, and sent his Hasidim to work in the transit camps (ma'abarot) and among the new immigrants in order to prevent the loss of their religious identity.[3, 8]
Chapter 9: Key Figures and International Connections
The leadership of the Rayatz was characterized by the ability to form alliances with various parties for the sake of the common goal. He did not shut himself up in the Hasidic court but acted as a pan-Jewish and international figure.[2, 3, 4]
These connections teach about the Rayatz's diplomatic conception: he saw the political tools of the modern world as heavenly means intended to serve the people of Israel.[24] This approach bequeathed to his successor the ability to act vis-à-vis heads of state and decision-makers throughout the world.[22]
Chapter 10: His Last Years and the Transition to the Leadership of the Rebbe
Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak passed away on the morning of the Sabbath, 10 Shevat 5711 (1950), at the world Chabad headquarters in New York.[7, 12] He left behind a movement that had risen from the ashes, educational institutions spread across the world, and above all – a generation of Hasidim imbued with the faith that "nothing is impossible".[3, 7] He was buried in the Chabad section of the Montefiore Cemetery in Queens, a place that has since become a pilgrimage site for millions of Jews (the "Ohel").[12]
After his passing, a gradual process began of the assumption of leadership by his son-in-law, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson.[5, 7] The Rebbe always emphasized that his work was a direct continuation of "the previous Rebbe" (der frierdiker Rebbe), and that the Rayatz is the "Nasi" (leader) who continues to lead the generation.[1, 5, 11]
The legacy of the Rayatz is measured not only by the number of books he wrote or the yeshivot he founded, but by the paradigm shift in modern Judaism. He turned Hasidism from a movement of Eastern Europe into a global and universal movement.[3, 22] He taught the Jewish world that there is no place too remote for the Torah, and no Jew too far for love.[22] His final victory was expressed decades later, when with the fall of the Iron Curtain it became clear that the underground network he had set up in Russia had not only survived but had become the basis on which modern Russian Jewry was rebuilt.[4, 5, 6]
Summary: The Leader Who Bridged an Abyss
In historical perspective, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was the right leader at the most right time.[3] He combined the spiritual strength of his forefathers with a modern capacity for political and organizational survival.[3, 6] His Torah teaching provided spiritual nourishment for a generation that had seen its world destroyed, and his practical work built the spiritual shelters in which the next generation would be able to grow.[3, 23]
He left behind an extensive literary legacy that to this day forms the backbone of the study of Hasidism in the world.[10, 25] From the theoretical "Sefer HaMaamarim" to the educational "Likkutei Dibburim," his writings continue to impart the message of Jewish pride, self-sacrifice and unceasing anticipation of the complete redemption.[10, 11] Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak proved that even when the body is bound in the chains of tyranny or paralyzed in a wheelchair, the Jewish spirit can break through boundaries, cross continents and change the face of history forever.[3, 6, 7]
